lead: A composite system is two or more qubits described together. Its state lives in a tensor-product space. Looking at only one part gives a reduced density matrix. That matrix can be mixed even when the whole system is pure. This idea is used in quantum communication, error correction and algorithms that measure one qubit while ignoring others. Density operators describe both pure and mixed states.
prereq: You need: 2.1, 2.3, 2.5, and tensor products from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A state vector |ψ⟩ works for a system known exactly. A mixed state is a classical probability distribution over pure states. You may know a qubit is |0⟩ with probability p and |1⟩ with probability 1-p, but not which. The density operator records that knowledge.

blocks.where: p_i ≥ 0 is the probability of pure state |ψ_i⟩; Σ_i p_i = 1; each |ψ_i⟩ is a unit vector; ρ is the density operator.

blocks.text: The matrix ρ is Hermitian, positive semidefinite, and has trace 1. The trace tr ρ is the sum of diagonal entries. For a measurement with projector P, the probability is tr(ρ P), not |amplitude|² alone.

Pure case: ρ=|ψ⟩⟨ψ|. Then ρ²=ρ and tr ρ²=1. Mixed case: tr ρ²<1. The number tr ρ² is the purity. It lies between 1/d and 1 for a d-level system. A pure state has one nonzero eigenvalue, equal to 1. A mixed state has at least two nonzero eigenvalues. Some syllabi call this topic density operators. Density matrices are needed when the preparation is uncertain or when part of a larger system is ignored.

When A and B are separate, their joint Hilbert space is H_A ⊗ H_B. Here H_A is the state space of A and H_B is the state space of B. Basis vectors are |i⟩_A ⊗ |j⟩_B, written |ij⟩. For two qubits the basis is 00, 01, 10, 11, so the dimension is 2×2=4. A pure joint state is |ψ⟩_AB = Σ_{i,j} c_{ij} |ij⟩. Here c_{ij} is a complex amplitude and Σ_{i,j} |c_{ij}|² = 1.

If |ψ⟩_AB = |φ⟩_A ⊗ |χ⟩_B, the state is a product. If no such factorization exists, it is entangled; see 2.7. The density matrix of a pure joint state is ρ_AB=|ψ⟩⟨ψ|. A local operator on A alone is O_A⊗I_B, where O_A acts on A and I_B is the identity on B. Its expected value is tr(ρ_AB (O_A⊗I_B)).
To predict statistics on A alone, you do not need the full joint state. You need its reduced state. The reduced state is the only part of ρ_AB that affects measurements made on A.
Choose an orthonormal basis {|j⟩_B} for B. The reduced state of A is the partial trace over B.

blocks.where: I_A is the identity on A; the sum runs over the B basis; ρ_A acts only on H_A; tr_B means trace over B.

blocks.text: In block-matrix form, write ρ_AB with blocks labelled by B. The partial trace keeps the diagonal blocks and sums them. It removes B. It is linear. It is not the full trace; a full trace would remove both systems and give a number.

The reduced state gives every measurement statistic on A: tr(ρ_A O_A)=tr(ρ_AB (O_A⊗I_B)). If ρ_AB is a product state, ρ_A is pure. If ρ_AB is pure and entangled, ρ_A can be mixed. For an entangled pair, no ket describes A alone. You must use the density matrix. The Bell pair example below gives ρ_A=I/2. That matrix has two equal diagonal entries and no off-diagonal terms.

figure.caption: The Bell pair's density matrix has four entries of 0.5. Keeping only the two diagonal blocks (B = 0 and B = 1) and adding them leaves ρ_A = I/2 with trace 1.0 and purity 0.5, so A is in a mixed state.

spec.title: Partial trace of a Bell pair
spec.aria: A pure Bell pair is written as a 4×4 density matrix with four entries of 0.5; summing the diagonal B = 0 block (0.5 top left) and B = 1 block (0.5 bottom right) gives ρ_A = I/2, trace 1.0 and purity 0.5, a mixed state.

examples.question: For |Φ+⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 in the basis {|00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩}: (a) write ρ_AB; (b) trace out B and find ρ_A; (c) show that ρ_A is mixed.
steps: Normalise: the coefficient is 1/√2. The pure density matrix is ρ_AB = |Φ+⟩⟨Φ+| = 1/2(|00⟩⟨00| + |00⟩⟨11| + |11⟩⟨00| + |11⟩⟨11|).
Trace over B with basis j=0,1: ρ_A = (I_A⊗⟨0|_B)ρ_AB(I_A⊗|0⟩_B) + (I_A⊗⟨1|_B)ρ_AB(I_A⊗|1⟩_B).
For j=0 the surviving diagonal block is [[0.5,0],[0,0]]. For j=1 the surviving diagonal block is [[0,0],[0,0.5]]. Their sum is ρ_A = [[0.5,0],[0,0.5]] = I/2, where I is the 2×2 identity.
Check purity: tr ρ_A² = 0.5² + 0.5² = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5. Since 0.5 < 1, ρ_A is mixed, not a pure ket.
examples.answer: The reduced state is ρ_A = I/2: trace 1.0, diagonal entries 0.5 and 0.5, purity 0.5, so it is mixed.
examples.check:
rho = [[0.0]*4 for _ in range(4)]
rho[0][0] = 0.5
rho[0][3] = 0.5
rho[3][0] = 0.5
rho[3][3] = 0.5
rhoA = [[0.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]]
for i in range(2):
    for k in range(2):
        for j in range(2):
            rhoA[i][k] += rho[2*i+j][2*k+j]
tr = rhoA[0][0] + rhoA[1][1]
purity = 0.0
for i in range(2):
    for j in range(2):
        purity += rhoA[i][j] * rhoA[j][i]
print(tr)
print(rhoA[0][0])
print(rhoA[1][1])
print(purity)

traps: Writing a ket for the reduced state of an entangled pair. A reduced state can be mixed and needs a density matrix.
Confusing ρ_AB with ρ_A⊗ρ_B. For an entangled state the joint density matrix is not a product of the two reduced states.
Using the full trace instead of the partial trace. Trace out only B to get ρ_A.
Saying ρ²=ρ always. Only pure density matrices are projectors; mixed states have tr ρ²<1.
Mixing probabilities p_i with amplitudes c_{ij}. Probabilities are nonnegative and sum to 1; amplitudes are complex and their moduli squared sum to 1.

quiz.q: What is the trace of every density operator?
State the condition for a density matrix to describe a pure state.
Why can the reduced state of one qubit be mixed when the two-qubit state is pure?
quiz.a: Information is lost when only local statistics on A are kept. Entanglement makes those local statistics look like a classical mixture.

quiz.q: For |Ψ−⟩ = (|01⟩ − |10⟩)/√2, find ρ_A after tracing out B.
If ρ_AB = ρ_A⊗ρ_B and both factors are pure, what is tr ρ_A²?
quiz.a: tr ρ_A² = 1. A product pure state has a pure reduced state on each side.

quiz.q: Why does ρ_A give the same measurement statistics on A as ρ_AB?
quiz.a: The partial trace is built so that tr(ρ_A O_A) = tr(ρ_AB (O_A⊗I_B)) for every operator O_A on A.

beyond: Not for the exam. Reduced density matrices are the working language of quantum information. Entanglement entropy is S(ρ_A) = −tr(ρ_A log₂ ρ_A); it is zero for product states and 1 for a Bell pair. Quantum error correction tracks how noise on physical qubits appears in reduced states of logical qubits. Open-system dynamics and decoherence use mixed states and channels. Search terms: reduced density matrix, entanglement entropy, quantum channel, Lindblad equation.
